1. Introduction

JDOOM (Black-Tech Browser) is a Chromium 153 fork that embeds port-probing capabilities directly into the browser engine. Unlock ports. Let the browser speak non-Web protocols. If it’s a web page, render it. If it’s a service, identify it. Say goodbye to installing a pile of clients and typing into dark terminals — every IP:Port you type into the address bar is automatically analysed.

Designed for security analysts, ops engineers, and developers, JDOOM turns the browser into a lightweight reconnaissance tool for authorized asset inventory and security auditing.

2. System Requirements & Installation

2.1 System Requirements

  • Windows 10 / 11 (x64)
  • Visual C++ Redistributable 2015-2022 (bundled with installer)
  • Minimum 4 GB RAM, 500 MB disk space

2.2 Installation (Installer EXE)

Run the Inno Setup installer. It includes the VC++ runtime and provides a standard uninstall experience. Follow the on-screen prompts to complete installation.

2.3 Source Patch

For advanced users: a diff patch against Chromium 153 source is available, along with full build parameters for self-compilation.

3. Quick Start

After launching JDOOM, simply type an IP:Port combination into the address bar — for example, 192.168.1.1:22 — and press Enter. JDOOM will automatically run its three-stage detection pipeline and display results.

chrome://jdoom
Figure 1 — JDOOM Settings page (chrome://jdoom). Configure timeouts and toggle detection stages here.

3.1 Normal Web Page Rendering

JDOOM is first and foremost a fully functional modern browser. For standard web services over HTTP/HTTPS, its rendering pipeline is identical to stock Chromium: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, multimedia and modern page layouts are all supported natively with no extra configuration. The figure below shows JDOOM rendering https://jiwo.org directly; tables, colors, images and CJK typography all display correctly, indistinguishable from any mainstream browser.

Only when the kernel determines a target port to be a non-web service does JDOOM switch to the probing pipeline described in Section 4; the web/non-web distinction is made automatically with no user intervention.

https://jiwo.org
Figure 2 — JDOOM natively rendering https://jiwo.org (a normal web page, just like any browser).

4. Three-Stage Detection Pipeline

JDOOM’s Visit = Probe engine probes ALL ports — including standard Web ports (80, 443, 8080) — executing three stages of increasing intensity. Each stage can independently produce a result, and the pipeline stops as soon as a conclusive answer is found — minimising network traffic and avoiding service disruption. Standard Web ports use shorter timeouts (connect 2 s, banner 800 ms, response 3 s) to keep the Web experience smooth; if a non-HTTP service happens to run on a standard port, the probe still returns a correct detection report rather than a failure.

Stage 1 — Read Active Banners

Passive Banner Capture

Many services proactively send a banner upon connection: SSH, FTP, SMTP, and Telnet are typical examples. JDOOM quietly reads these banners without sending any data, then stops. This stage completes in milliseconds and has zero impact on the target service.

Stage 2 — Try HTTP

Web Page or Protocol Mismatch

If no banner is received, JDOOM attempts an HTTP request. If the port serves a real website, it renders the full page exactly as a normal browser would. If the response indicates a non-HTTP protocol, the pipeline advances to Stage 3.

Stage 3 — Service Fingerprinting

Protocol-Specific Handshake Probes

For non-web ports, JDOOM sends minimal protocol-specific handshake packets to identify the running service. See the table below for supported protocols.

Service Fingerprint Matrix

RDP (Remote Desktop)3389X.224 Connection Request
SQL Server (TDS)1433TDS Prelogin
SMB (File Sharing)445 / 139SMB1 + SMB2 Negotiate
SunRPC / Portmap135 / 111GETPORT Call
SSL/TLS (Implicit)465 / 993 / 995 / 636TLS ClientHello
127.0.0.1:8021

5. Probe Report Page

Every detection result is displayed on the built-in Probe Report page at chrome://jdoom-probe. The report includes:

  • Service type and protocol identification
  • Banner text (with escaped bytes for non-printable characters)
  • Hexadecimal raw data for manual inspection
  • Response time for each stage
  • One-click jump to Telnet terminal for interactive sessions

7. Interactive Telnet Terminal

JDOOM includes a full-featured Telnet client at chrome://jdoom-telnet, built on Chromium's net::TCPClientSocket. It is a real TCP client — not a JavaScript emulation.

7.1 Key Features

  • IAC protocol stripping — WILL / WONT / DO / DONT negotiations are handled automatically.
  • Basic ANSI colour support for terminal output.
  • One-click jump from any probe result page.
  • URL parameters ?host=&port= for auto-connect.
chrome://jdoom-telnet
Figure 7 — Telnet terminal interface (chrome://jdoom-telnet).
chrome://jdoom-telnet — 202.5.197.3:23
Figure 8 — Live Telnet session connected to a ZTE ZXR10 router at 202.5.197.3:23.

7.2 Usage

Navigate to chrome://jdoom-telnet, enter the target host and port, and press Connect. You can also click the "Open Telnet" button on any probe result page to jump directly into an interactive session.

Warning: The Telnet terminal sends data in cleartext. Only use it on networks and systems you are authorized to access.

8. Built-in Security Extensions

JDOOM ships with six built-in security extensions designed to assist with web debugging, security testing, and protocol analysis:

ExtensionPurpose
CharsetDetect and switch character encodings
Cookie-EditorView, create, edit, and delete cookies
Header ModifierInspect and modify HTTP request/response headers
JS ToggleEnable or disable JavaScript per tab
Markdown ViewerRender Markdown files directly in the browser
Proxy SwitchyOmega 3 (ZeroOmega)Manage and switch proxy configurations
Note: All built-in extensions have their onInstalled event suppressed — no extension onboarding popups or first-run UI on startup, ensuring a clean out-of-the-box experience. Tampermonkey is intentionally excluded to maintain a controlled extension environment.

9. Configurable Timeouts

All timeout values can be adjusted on the Settings page (chrome://jdoom):

  • Banner read timeout — how long to wait for an unsolicited banner.
  • HTTP probe timeout — how long to wait for an HTTP response.
  • Service fingerprint timeout — how long to wait for handshake replies.

Shorter timeouts speed up scanning of known-unresponsive hosts; longer timeouts improve accuracy on high-latency links.

10. Deployment Options

10.1 Installer EXE

The standard distribution is an Inno Setup installer that bundles the VC++ runtime. It provides a familiar install/uninstall experience and registers JDOOM in Add/Remove Programs.

10.2 Source Patch

For organisations that build their own Chromium: a patch set (diff) against Chromium 153 is provided, along with the complete GN/Ninja build parameters used to produce the official binaries.

10.3 Background Mode

JDOOM has disabled background mode. When the last browser window is closed, the process exits completely — no background process remains. This aligns with the security-first design philosophy: no hidden network connections linger.

11. Legal & Ethical Use

JDOOM's port-probing features are designed for authorized asset inventory and security auditing only. Always ensure you have explicit permission before probing any host or network. Unauthorized scanning may violate local laws and regulations.

12. Google Connection Blocking

JDOOM blocks all automatic connections to Google servers at the source-code level, eliminating data leakage at its root:

  • Version checks (Omaha)
  • Telemetry and metrics (UMA / UKM)
  • User feedback reporting
  • Crash reporting (Crashpad)
  • RLZ tracking identifiers
  • Component updates (Widevine CDM, etc.)
  • Account consistency checks (Dice / Mirror)
  • Safe Browsing

Chrome Web Store extension downloads remain unaffected — users can still install and manage extensions normally. Privacy-first is JDOOM’s core design principle.
